title: Cooperative Societies and Joint Stock Companies
summary: A voluntary association of persons who join together to protect and promote their common economic interests on the basis of equality and mutual help. Its main aim is service to members, not profit. Example: Amul (Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation), owned by lakhs of milk producers.

Characteristics: voluntary membership — anyone can join or leave; open membership irrespective of caste or religion; registration is compulsory (Cooperative Societies Act, 1912, or state Acts), with a minimum of ten members; separate legal entity and stable life — death, insolvency or insanity of members does not affect it; limited liability of members; democratic management — 'one man, one vote' whatever the number of shares; service motive; capital raised mainly from members' shares; surplus distributed as limited dividend and bonus on purchases.

Types: consumers' cooperatives (Kendriya Bhandar, Apna Bazar, Super Bazar — buy directly from producers and sell to members at fair prices); producers' cooperatives (handloom societies — supply raw materials and tools to small producers); marketing cooperatives (Amul — collect and sell members' products); thrift and credit cooperatives (village service societies, urban cooperative banks — accept deposits and give cheap loans); cooperative housing societies (build or buy houses for members at reasonable cost); cooperative farming societies.

Advantages: easy formation; limited liability; stable life; democratic control; service at low cost by eliminating middlemen; government help (loans, tax relief). Limitations: limited capital; inefficient management by honorary office-bearers; members lack zeal because they get only limited dividend and no extra reward for effort; conflicts among members; excessive government regulation; lack of secrecy.

A voluntary association of persons formed under the Companies Act, with a capital divided into transferable shares. Characteristics: artificial legal person created by law; separate legal entity — it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name; perpetual succession — members may come and go but the company continues; common seal; limited liability of shareholders to the unpaid value of their shares; transferability of shares (free in a public company); separation of ownership and management — shareholders own it, elected directors manage it; registration under the Companies Act is compulsory.

Private company: minimum 2 members (maximum 200 under the 2013 Act; 50 earlier), restrictions on transfer of shares, cannot invite the public to buy shares, at least 2 directors. Public company: minimum 7 members, no maximum, shares freely transferable, can issue a prospectus, at least 3 directors (e.g. Reliance Industries Ltd). Advantages: large capital; limited liability; perpetual succession; transferability of shares; professional management; scope for expansion and research. Limitations: difficult and costly formation; excessive legal control; lack of secrecy; delay in decisions; separation of ownership and control can lead to misuse by directors; conflict of interests.

A company in which at least 51% of the paid-up share capital is held by the central or a state government (or both). Examples: Coal India, ONGC, Indian Oil Corporation, SAIL, NTPC, MTNL. Features: separate legal entity registered under the Companies Act; all or most directors are appointed by the government; its accounts are audited under the Comptroller and Auditor General and the reports go to Parliament; it gets its funds from government and the public.

A company with its head office in one country and business operations (factories, branches, offices) in many countries — Hindustan Unilever, Nestle, Samsung, Coca-Cola, Hyundai, Suzuki. Advantages to the host country: inflow of foreign capital, latest technology, employment, better quality goods and wider choice, export promotion and foreign exchange, competition that pushes domestic producers to improve quality, and professional management. Limitations: they may harm small domestic industries, send large profits abroad, interfere in local politics, exploit natural resources and spread a foreign consumer culture.

objective: Fill in the blanks: (a) Indian Oil Corporation and ONGC are examples of ________. (b) The risk of loss in a company is spread over a large number of ________.

Write True (T) or False (F): (a) Death, bankruptcy or insanity of members does not affect the continuity of a cooperative society. (b) A cooperative society can be started with a minimum of 2 members.

(a) True — it has a separate legal entity and stable life.
(b) False — it needs at least 10 members.
Fill in the blanks: (a) The minimum paid-up capital to start a private limited company was ₹ ________. (b) The liability of the members of a cooperative society is ________.

(a) 1 lakh (under the Companies Act, 1956; the 2013 Act as amended has no minimum)
(b) limited

Write True (T) or False (F): (a) Domestic producers improve the quality of their products because of multinational companies. (b) It is necessary to get every company incorporated, whether private or public.

(a) True — competition from MNCs pushes them to improve.
(b) True — registration under the Companies Act is compulsory.
Mrs. Reeta is afraid that if her business assets fall short, her personal assets may be used to pay the debts. (a) Which form of organisation should she choose? (b) Why?

(a) A joint stock company.
(b) Its shareholders have limited liability — they lose at most the value of their shares; personal assets are safe.
vsa: 'Members may come and members may go, but the company continues to exist.' Identify and explain this feature of a joint stock company.

Perpetual succession. A company is a separate legal entity created by law, so its life is not affected by the death, insolvency, retirement or transfer of shares of any member. It ends only when it is wound up by law.
State any two features of a government company.

(1) At least 51% of its paid-up share capital is held by the central or state government.
(2) It is registered under the Companies Act and has a separate legal entity; its directors are mostly appointed by the government and its accounts are audited under the CAG.
State two disadvantages of a joint stock company.

(1) Difficult and expensive formation with many legal formalities.
(2) Lack of secrecy — accounts must be published.
(Also: delay in decisions; separation of ownership and control may lead to misuse.)

or: State two disadvantages of a multinational company.

(1) They may harm small domestic industries that cannot compete.
(2) They send large profits to their home country, causing an outflow of foreign exchange.
(Also: exploitation of natural resources; interference in local affairs.)

vsa: What is a thrift and credit cooperative society? Explain.

It is a cooperative formed to give financial help to its members. It collects small savings (thrift) from members as deposits and lends money to members in need at low rates of interest, saving them from moneylenders. Examples: village service cooperative societies, urban cooperative banks.
Explain any two features of cooperative societies.

(1) Voluntary and open membership — anyone with a common interest can join or leave freely.
(2) Democratic management — 'one man, one vote', whatever the number of shares held.
(Also: compulsory registration, limited liability, service motive, stable life.)

Vinod wants a business in which his personal assets cannot be used to pay business debts. Suggest a form. OR A cooperative set up in Chandigarh gives members houses and civic amenities at low cost. Identify its type.

Vinod: a joint stock company, whose members have limited liability.
The Chandigarh society is a cooperative (group) housing society.
sa: State any three limitations of a cooperative society.

(1) Limited capital — members are usually of small means and get only a limited dividend.
(2) Inefficient management — honorary office-bearers may lack business skill.
(3) Lack of motivation and conflicts among members; excessive government control. (Any three.)
State any three limitations of a joint stock company.

(1) Difficult and costly formation.
(2) Excessive government regulation and lack of secrecy.
(3) Delay in decision-making and possible misuse of power by directors because ownership is separate from management. (Any three.)
What is meant by a private company? State three of its features.

A company that restricts the transfer of its shares and does not invite the public to buy them.
(1) Minimum 2 and maximum 200 members (50 under the old Act).
(2) Restriction on transfer of shares.
(3) Cannot issue a prospectus; needs at least 2 directors and can start business on getting the certificate of incorporation.
Joint stock company: explain (a) perpetual succession (b) separation of ownership and management.

(a) Perpetual succession: the company has its own existence; the death, insolvency or exit of members does not affect it.
(b) Separation of ownership and management: shareholders own the company but, being many and scattered, they elect a board of directors who manage it.
Why do members of a cooperative society not work with full zeal? Explain along with other limitations.

Members get only a limited dividend on capital and no extra reward for extra effort, and office-bearers are often honorary — so there is little personal motivation.
Other limitations: limited capital; inefficient management; conflicts among members; excessive government control; lack of secrecy.
la: Amul is an Indian dairy cooperative formed in 1946 and owned by 3.6 million producers in Gujarat; it led India's white revolution. (a) What is a cooperative society? (b) Why was Amul promoted as a cooperative? Explain four merits of the cooperative form.

(a) A cooperative society is a voluntary association of persons who join together on the basis of equality to promote their common economic interest, with service to members as its main aim.
(b) Small milk producers could not sell profitably alone and were exploited by middlemen; together they could collect, process and market milk themselves. Merits:
(1) Elimination of middlemen — producers get a fair price.
(2) Democratic management — one man, one vote, so every producer has a say.
(3) Limited liability and stable life — unaffected by death or exit of members.
(4) Government support and easy formation; service at low cost to members.

What are multinational companies? Give two examples and explain any four advantages.

A multinational company has its head office in one country and operates factories or offices in several other countries. Examples: Hindustan Unilever, Nestle, Samsung, Coca-Cola.
(1) Inflow of foreign capital into the host country.
(2) Latest technology and research.
(3) Employment opportunities.
(4) Better quality goods and wider choice for consumers; competition improves domestic products.
(5) Export promotion and foreign exchange earnings.

Explain any three advantages and two limitations of joint stock companies.

Advantages: (1) Large capital from many shareholders. (2) Limited liability encourages investment. (3) Perpetual succession and transferability of shares; professional management.
Limitations: (1) Difficult, costly formation and excessive legal control. (2) Delay in decisions and lack of secrecy.
October 2024
Distinguish between a private limited and a public limited company on any five bases.

Minimum members: 2 vs 7.
Maximum members: 200 (50 earlier) vs no limit.
Transfer of shares: restricted vs free.
Prospectus: cannot invite the public vs can issue a prospectus.
Directors: at least 2 vs at least 3.
Commencement of business: on incorporation vs (earlier) after a certificate of commencement.
April 2019
What is a joint stock company? Explain any four of its characteristics.

A voluntary association of persons formed under the Companies Act with capital divided into transferable shares.
(1) Artificial legal person and separate legal entity.
(2) Perpetual succession.
(3) Limited liability of shareholders.
(4) Transferability of shares.
(5) Separation of ownership and management; common seal; compulsory registration.

What are the activities of a consumers' cooperative society? Explain four features of cooperative societies.

A consumers' cooperative buys goods in bulk directly from producers or wholesalers and sells them to members (and others) at reasonable prices, removing middlemen; profit is shared as a bonus on purchases. Examples: Kendriya Bhandar, Apna Bazar.
Features: (1) voluntary, open membership; (2) compulsory registration with at least ten members; (3) democratic control — one man, one vote; (4) service motive; also limited liability and separate legal entity.
